titulo: Weekly Test 5 — Quoting evidence, text structure, point of view, word roots and arguments

bloques.html: Instructions: Read each question carefully. For multiple-choice questions, mark the letter of the correct answer with an ✗. When a question asks you to quote, copy the exact words from the text inside quotation marks. We start with Listening: an adult will read a short podcast aloud twice.

bloques.html:
Read the story and answer questions 6 to 8.

The New Kid

I decided I didn't like Rafael the moment he walked into our classroom. He didn't smile. He didn't say hello. He sat in the back and stared out the window at the rain as if the rest of us weren't there.

"He thinks he's too good for us," I whispered to Sofía. She shrugged.

For a week I watched him. He ate lunch alone. He never raised his hand. When Ms. Vera asked him to read aloud, he shook his head, and she let him be. I was sure that proved it: he was rude.

Then on Friday I forgot my umbrella. I stood under the roof by the gate while the rain came down in sheets. Rafael walked past, stopped, and came back. He held out his umbrella without a word.

"I have a bike," he said finally, slowly, as if each word cost him something. "You take it."

I noticed then that his accent was different. Later Sofía told me his family had arrived from Haiti in March. He had been learning our language for only four months.

I had spent a week deciding what Rafael was. I had never once asked him.

alternativas.html: A classmate of Rafael whose name we don't know

bloques.html: Who is telling the story? (1 pt)

pauta.respuesta: C) A classmate of Rafael whose name we don't know
pauta.oa: CCSS RL.5.6 — punto de vista del narrador

alternativas.html: We know everything Rafael thinks and feels.
We only see Rafael through the narrator's opinions, and those opinions turn out to be wrong.
We learn the story from Rafael's family.
We know what Ms. Vera thinks about him.

bloques.html: How does the narrator's point of view affect what we know about Rafael? (1 pt)

pauta.respuesta: B) We only see Rafael through the narrator's opinions, and those turn out to be wrong
pauta.oa: RL.5.6 — cómo el punto de vista afecta la narración

bloques.html:
Read the text and answer questions 9 to 11.

The Frog That Hides in Its Father's Throat

Deep in the forests of southern Chile lives one of the strangest animals on Earth: Darwin's frog. It is tiny, about the size of a 100-peso coin, and it looks exactly like a dead leaf. But its most surprising feature is how it raises its young. After the eggs hatch, the father swallows the tadpoles into a pouch in his throat. There they grow for several weeks, safe from predators, until the father opens his mouth and tiny frogs hop out.

For thousands of years, this plan worked well. Today, however, Darwin's frog is disappearing. There are two main causes. First, the native forests where the frog lives have been cut down to make space for farms and tree plantations. Without the damp forest floor, the frogs dry out and die. Second, a fungus that attacks the skin of frogs arrived in Chile. Because frogs breathe partly through their skin, the fungus can kill them in weeks.

Scientists are fighting back. In Concepción and Santiago, zoos have built special rooms where frogs breed safely, far from the fungus. Other groups are working with farmers to protect pieces of native forest. Nobody knows yet whether these efforts will be enough, but every year more young frogs are released into the wild.

alternativas.html: Describing the frog's body from head to tail
Presenting a problem and then solutions
Comparing Darwin's frog with other frogs
Telling events in the order they happened

bloques.html: How does the author organize paragraphs 2 and 3 together? (1 pt)

pauta.respuesta: B) Presenting a problem and then solutions

alternativas.html: The frogs dry out and die.
Tadpoles grow in the father's throat.

bloques.html: According to paragraph 2, what is the effect of cutting down native forests? (1 pt)

pauta.respuesta: B) The frogs dry out and die

pauta.oa: OA10-13 / Flyers Speaking — opinar, describir un proceso, narrar

pautaHtml:
Guion de Listening (leer dos veces, en voz alta)

Lee a ritmo normal, como un podcast. Pausa de 30 segundos entre lecturas. No expliques palabras. Este texto es más denso que los anteriores: es el techo del año.

The Cold River in the Sea

Imagine standing on a beach in northern Chile in the middle of summer. The sun is burning, but when you step into the sea, the water is freezing. Why? The answer is a giant river inside the ocean called the Humboldt Current. It carries cold water from near Antarctica all the way up the coast of Chile and Peru.

This cold water does something remarkable. It rises from the deep and brings up nutrients, tiny bits of food that feed enormous clouds of plankton. Plankton feeds small fish like anchovies, anchovies feed bigger fish, and the bigger fish feed sea lions, penguins, and millions of seabirds. Because of this, the Humboldt Current is one of the richest fishing areas on the planet, even though it covers less than one percent of the ocean.

The current also explains why the Atacama is the driest desert in the world. Cold water cools the air above it, and cool air holds very little moisture. Clouds form, but they almost never release rain. So the same cold current that fills the sea with life keeps the land beside it almost empty of it.

Guion de Speaking (4-5 minutos)

Solo en inglés. Tres tareas cortas; no corrijas durante la conversación. Califica al final.

  1. Warm-up (20 s, no se califica): "Hi! How was your week?"
  2. Opinion (1,5 min): "Do you think it is important to learn more than one language? Give me two reasons. What would someone who disagrees say?" Apoyo: "Can you give an example from your life?"
  3. Process (1,5 min): "Imagine a new student arrives at your class and doesn't speak the language well. Explain, step by step, what you would do to make them feel welcome." Apoyo: "What would you do first?" / "And after that?"
  4. Story (1,5 min): "Tell me about a time someone surprised you, or a time you were wrong about a person. What did you think at first, what happened, and what did you learn?"
  5. Cierre: "Thank you, that's all."

Rúbricas

Argumento escrito (ítem 15) — máximo 6 puntos:

Criterio Puntos
Afirmación (claim) clara en la primera o segunda oración 1
Dos razones distintas; al menos una con ejemplo o explicación (1 pt por razón bien desarrollada, máximo 2) 2
Contraargumento reconocido ("Some people say...") y respondido ("However...") 1
Organización: claim → razones → contraargumento → conclusión, con conectores; 8-10 oraciones 1
Gramática, ortografía y puntuación: máximo 3 errores en total 1

Speaking (ítem 16) — cada criterio 0, 1 o 2 puntos:

Criterio 2 pts 1 pt 0 pts
Contenido Cumple las tres tareas: opinión con 2 razones y contraargumento, proceso con pasos claros, historia con sus tres partes y aprendizaje Cumple dos tareas completas o las tres de forma incompleta Una tarea o menos
Organización Ideas en orden con conectores variados (first, because, however, then, in the end, that's why) Orden confuso o conectores repetitivos Sin estructura
Vocabulario Rico y preciso para la edad; incluye expresiones de opinión y contraste (I believe, on the other hand, even though) Repite palabras básicas o cambia a español en 1-2 palabras Muy limitado; mezcla español con frecuencia
Corrección Tiempos verbales variados (pasado, condicional "would", presente perfecto) y concordancia correctos casi siempre (máximo 2 errores) Varios errores que no impiden entender Errores constantes

Qué mira este instrumento

Fase C, techo del año: Common Core ELA Grade 5 completo. Comprensión auditiva de un texto informativo denso con relación causa-efecto e interpretación de una frase (1-5); narración en primera persona: punto de vista y cita textual para sustentar inferencia (6-8, RL.5.1 y RL.5.6); texto informativo: estructura problema-solución, causa-efecto y dos ideas principales (9-11, RI.5.2, RI.5.3, RI.5.5); raíces latinas y modismos (12-14, L.5.4b y L.5.5b); argumento escrito con contraargumento (15, W.5.1); speaking con tres tareas (16).

Este instrumento está por sobre el currículum chileno de Inglés 5º (que apunta a A1-A2) y se justifica solo por el perfil bilingüe del niño; un resultado de 60-70% aquí es bueno. Señales: si falla 7 u 8, aún no separa "lo que dice el narrador" de "lo que es verdad", la habilidad más fina de lectura narrativa en 5º. Si falla 9 u 11, lee párrafo a párrafo pero no ve la arquitectura del texto. Si 15 pierde el punto de contraargumento, es lo esperable: es la parte más difícil de W.5.1 y se enseña explícitamente.

Si le fue mal

  • Citar evidencia: con cada afirmación que haga sobre un libro, exigir "show me where it says that" y que lea la frase en voz alta antes de explicar.
  • Punto de vista: recontar un cuento conocido desde otro personaje ("tell me the story as if you were the wolf").
  • Estructura del texto: antes de leer un texto informativo, mirar títulos y palabras señal (because, however, first) y predecir cómo está organizado; después confirmar.
  • Raíces: una raíz por día en la pared (bio, geo, tele, aud, spect, port, dict, rupt) con tres palabras cada una.
  • Argumento: debate oral de 3 minutos a la hora de comer sobre un tema simple; el niño debe decir "some people think..., however..." al menos una vez.
